Abia State has recorded a 60 per cent reduction in maternal mortality between 2024 and 2026, emerging as the state with the second-lowest maternal mortality rate nationwide. The Commissioner for Information, Okey Kanu, disclosed this on Monday at Government House, Umuahia, while briefing journalists on the outcome of this week’s State Executive Council meeting presided over by Governor Alex Otti. Kanu, who was represented by the Special Adviser to the Governor on Media and Publicity, Ferdinand Ekeoma, attributed the improvement to ongoing reforms in the health sector. “Abia State has recorded a 60 per cent reduction in maternal mortality between 2024 and 2026. This reflects our commitment to strengthening healthcare delivery and expanding access to quality medical services for our mothers and children,” he said. He disclosed that 190 of the 200 Project Ekwueme Primary Healthcare Centres earmarked for renovation had been renovated, while 123 had been functionalised to provide essential healthcare services. “190 out of the 200 Project Ekwueme Primary Healthcare Centres have been renovated, and 123 have been functionalised to provide essential healthcare services to our people,” he stated. Kanu further announced that the National Nursing and Midwifery Council, in its accreditation report released on November 13, had increased the admission quota of the Aba Campus of the College of Nursing Sciences from 75 to 120 students. “The increase in admission capacity reflects growing recognition of the state’s investments and reforms in the health sector, particularly in strengthening healthcare manpower development,” he said. In another development, Kanu announced that the Rector of Ogbonnaya Onu Polytechnic, Aba, Dr Christopher Okoro, had emerged Administrator of the Year in a nationwide poll conducted by the Leadership Excellence Award. He said Okoro polled 148,267 votes in the exercise, which recognised his contributions to institutional transformation, human capital development, and technical and professional education. “Dr Okoro polled 148,267 votes. They cited his contributions to institutional transformation, human capital development, and technical and professional education in Abia State,” he said. Kanu said the recognition reflected ongoing changes at the institution, citing increased student enrolment of over 6,000, infrastructure improvements and enhanced workers’ welfare as some of the achievements recorded under the rector’s leadership. He reaffirmed that the Otti administration remained committed to sustaining its development agenda, adding that the education sector continued to receive 20 per cent of the state’s budgetary allocation, with the impact being felt across the education ecosystem. On public health surveillance, Kanu disclosed that no cases of diseases of public health importance, including Ebola, Lassa fever, COVID-19, diphtheria, cholera, mpox and yellow fever, were reported in Abia during the period under review. Contributing, the Commissioner for Health, Professor Enoch Ogbonnay-Uche, spoke on the Ebola situation in the country and disclosed that the index case reported on October 20 had been transferred to Switzerland, where the patient subsequently recovered. “All 62 contacts traced to the index case had completed the mandatory 21-day monitoring period and were cleared as of November 13, according to information from the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control (NCDC),” Professor Uche said. He urged residents to remain vigilant and maintain good personal hygiene, stressing that sustained public awareness and preventive measures were essential to safeguarding public health. Professor Uche emphasised the importance of hand hygiene, which he identified as the focus of the state’s public health advisory for the week. “This week, the health advisory focuses on hand hygiene. Hand hygiene is very important in preventing infection. We want to ensure that in this season, people wash their hands regularly with running water,” he stated. He explained that hand hygiene remained one of the simplest and most effective ways of preventing infections and reducing the spread of communicable diseases.
